summary:
Louisiana stands under the United States national framework on travel documents and entry. Executive Order 14168, effective January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth, and new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted. Passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until they expire, but trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The American Civil Liberties Union has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on documentation and on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court has allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports. A trans visitor entering Louisiana can therefore expect documents that do not match their presentation.

Visa exposure is a separate matter. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code SWS25. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently. Airport screening carries a further disclosure risk: the National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to Transportation Security Administration officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening of the type matching one's presentation.

Violence risk in Louisiana is measured independently of its legal position. Louisiana records the highest per-capita killing rate of trans women of any state: 24.7 per 100,000 trans women per year on a reported basis, with 19 recorded cases, against 23.5 for the state that ranks highest on legal-safety measures. The figures rest on a base of 428 United States victims across 2008 to 2025, and every figure is an undercount floor rather than a total. The analysis reporting the rate cautions that legal-risk rankings do not sort physical safety, and notes that the states holding the worst legal positions hold the highest measured killing rates.

The attack on a trans couple in August 2026 shows how that risk interacts with local procedure. Aurora Rush and Shae Sanders were beaten by a mob at Cypress Black Bayou Park in Benton over restroom use. Sanders, who has a pre-existing spinal injury, and Rush, who sustained a concussion and blood pooling, were both charged with disturbing the peace while no attacker was arrested. Rush was denied hospital care, was jailed in a men's facility and was searched by a male guard despite a 'female' marker on her driver's licence. The plea deal offered to the couple had not been signed. The municipality simultaneously voted one of the country's most severe anti-trans restroom ordinances, and the Sheriff's Office confirmed that no one else was arrested that day.

Custody exposure for trans residents of Louisiana is documented and deadly. Yella (Robert) Clark Jr., a 45-year-old Black trans woman serving a life sentence at Angola prison, was killed in a fight with several inmates on 2 April 2024. Her death was at least the 16th killing of a trans or gender-expansive person recorded by the Human Rights Campaign that year and the fifth that April alone. Deaths of trans and gender-expansive people in custody are systematically under- or mis-reported, so the recorded count understates the pattern.
tangentialFactors:
Facility use is regulated by state law across the country in ways that bear on where a trans visitor can safely go. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in kindergarten-to-grade-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use according to gender identity; in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement is documented: in April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at the state capitol of one southeastern state was arrested and handcuffed, which civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Identity-document rules are the fastest-moving area of state restriction. One midwestern state has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, and rights groups describe that statute as a template other legislatures are following, with further targeting bills pending. The Movement Advancement Project maintains a state-by-state map setting out which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions, so the rules a visitor or resident encounters depend heavily on the state involved.

Foreign governments have issued public warnings about travelling to the United States. At least eight foreign countries, including two in northern Europe, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country after the federal document and data rules took effect, and those advisories followed detentions of foreign citizens over visa issues.

A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies one northwestern state as the latest flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends. The same assessment cautions that legal-risk rankings do not sort physical safety, which is consistent with Louisiana's position: it holds the highest measured killing rate of trans women of any state while the killing rate, not the statute book, drives that figure.
localsOnly:
Louisiana's own identity-document position is not set out in the material available here. The national framework governs federal passports, while state-issued documents such as Louisiana driver's licences and Louisiana birth certificates are governed by state law, and the Movement Advancement Project maintains the state-by-state map of which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes and under what conditions. A resident checking their own documents should use that map rather than assume the federal position applies to them.

Local regulation in Louisiana can be more restrictive than state law. In Benton, the municipality voted one of the country's most severe anti-trans restroom ordinances in August 2026, at the same time as the mob attack on Aurora Rush and Shae Sanders at Cypress Black Bayou Park. Local ordinances of that kind can restrict facility access in municipal parks and buildings even where state law is silent or less restrictive.

The conduct of custody authorities is a documented risk for trans residents. When Aurora Rush was jailed after the Benton attack, she was placed in a men's facility and searched by a male guard despite the 'female' marker on her driver's licence, and she was denied hospital care before being taken there. Yella (Robert) Clark Jr., a 45-year-old Black trans woman serving a life sentence at Angola prison, was killed by other inmates on 2 April 2024. Deaths of trans and gender-expansive people in custody are systematically under- or mis-reported, so official counts understate the pattern.

Charging decisions can fall on victims rather than attackers. Rush and Sanders were charged with disturbing the peace while no attacker was arrested, and the Sheriff's Office confirmed that no one else was arrested that day. Civil-rights attorneys who reviewed the case noted that the plea deal offered had not been signed.
outOfScopeNotes:
Louisiana's statewide rules on gender-marker changes for driver's licences and birth certificates are unresolved in the available material. The federal passport position is documented, but no source here sets out what Louisiana itself permits, and the Movement Advancement Project's map is the reference for that question.

Louisiana's own facility-use law is unresolved here. The national inventory records bathroom bans in force in nine states and one territory without naming which, and records twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia with no ban; Louisiana's placement between those positions is not stated in the material available.

Whether Louisiana appears on the four-state do-not-travel list identified in the legal risk assessment of 13 July 2026 is unresolved. That assessment names only the most recently flagged state, and the sources do not disclose the composition of the list.

The 24.7 per 100,000 trans women killing figure is derived from reported cases and is explicitly an undercount floor. The source does not state how many of the 19 recorded cases are confirmed as anti-trans homicides by a court or investigation, nor how Louisiana's rate compares on a per-capita basis to smaller states where a single case moves the rate sharply.

The circumstances of the Angola killing of 2 April 2024 are documented only as a fight involving several inmates. Whether disciplinary, protective or housing failures contributed to the death is not sourced here, and the Human Rights Campaign memorial is not a court finding.

No source here addresses hate-crime charging, prosecution outcomes or sentence in the Benton mob attack, the terms of the plea deal offered, or the status of the disturbing-the-peace charges against Rush and Sanders. Nor is there material on Louisiana-specific access to gender-affirming care, on Louisiana's treatment of foreign national detainees, or on visa refusal rates for visitors travelling to Louisiana specifically.
